There are plenty of monosyllables, whether original monosyllables or not I cannot say. There are also plenty of dissyllables, the marked feature of which is that they always carry the Low Tone and the neutral vowel -ə. The initial consonant in these unaccented syllables is never aspirated [interlinear insertion: (if we except -sᶜ-, which is always aspirated as in Shan, not in Burma)], & is practically confined to k-, ts-, t-, p-, r- & sᶜ-. ... There are indications that these final consonants, being in unaccented syllables, tend to drop off, leaving merely the neutral vowel." new_statements.quote: Luce ms p. 053: "Unaccented Penultimates. The accent in R.L. always falls on the last syllable. There are plenty of monosyllables, whether original monosyllables or not I cannot say. There are also plenty of dissyllables, the marked feature of which is that they always carry the Low Tone and the neutral vowel -ə." Shorto 2013 p. ii: "The pitch of prefixial syllables is always low, and this is not specially marked. Low pitch is probably generally connected with absence of stress; it is frequent in particles and the first syllables of compounds". Hall 2018 p. 83: "Riang Lang is sesquisyllabic; words include a main syllable and an optional reduced syllable preceding the main syllable ... The reduced syllable has a limited inventory of consonants, and vowel and tone are neutralized."

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (image-only scan, 4 pp; rendered PDF p. 3 = NLA footer "Luce Collection, MS 6547, Box 7, Folder 64, Page 053") and read the handwriting myself. The heading "Unaccented Penultimates." and the passage are there as quoted: "The accent in R.L. always falls on the [one word struck out] last syllable. There are plenty of monosyllables, whether original monosyllables or not I cannot say. There are also plenty of dissyllables, the marked feature of which is that they always carry the Low Tone and the neutral vowel -ə." The continuation matches the reader's paraphrase (initials of unaccented syllables never aspirated, confined to k-, ts-, t-, p-, r-, s'-; finals -k, -ŋ, -n, -m, -r, rarely -l,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Riang Lang is a two-tone language with sesquisyllabic words: a full main syllable optionally preceded by one reduced (prefixal/minor) syllable with a neutral vowel and no tone contrast. Word accent/stress falls on the main syllable, which is always the last syllable of the word; the preceding minor syllable is unaccented (low pitch, neutral vowel, reduced consonant inventory, final consonants tending to drop). Effectively fixed final (= main-syllable) stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for word accent. Luce (ms p. 050) notes some common words seem to have no fixed tone; Shorto (p. ii) notes low pitch also in particles and first syllables of compounds and 'disturbance of lexical tone' in doubled roots.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, based on elicited wordlists (Luce's field notes, 1930s-50s; Hall's 1537-item list from Sam Kha village, Namsang township, 2015-17). Luce's statement is an unpublished manuscript note; Hall 2018, the only Glottolog-listed description, never uses the word stress and describes only tone and sesquisyllabic structure.
new_statements.identity_note: All three statements concern Riang Lang = Yinnet / Black Riang (ISO ril, rian1261): Luce's 'R.L.' is Riang-Lang (his Riang Sak/Riang Lai material is the sister variety Yinchia, ISO yin, glottocode yinc1238). Hall 2018 describes the Riang Lang of Sam Kha village, Namsang township, southern Shan State; Luce's notes come from his own 1930s-50s fieldwork (informant U San Mya for the Riang Sak-Riang Lang lexicon); Shintani 2014 (not seen) covers a Riang Lang variety near Löy Lëm, Panglong. Riang Lang and Riang Lai are reported mutually intelligible.
